chapter: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
title: Big Jim Colosimo's murder and the start of gangster Chicago
summary: As a high school student working downtown he saw the beginnings of Capone's Mafia after Colosimo was assassinated; Prohibition did no harm to musicians' work.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: And that must have been very rough, well, really the gangster days hadn't begun when you left.

They were just beginning because I was working downtown during my vacation off from high school when this guy, Big Jim Collinsimo, had a place down on Wabash Avenue and I think it was around 23rd Street -- Big Jim Colisemo. Old Eddie South Softan worked a lot of them, worked there, and when they got Al Capone from Brooklyn here, that's where the seat of the Mafia was started there, because Big Jim Colisimo was Italian, and they moved in there. That's when Capone came from New York, Brooklyn to Chicago.

Now Frankie Yale was the leader to the Capones, but he never got along too good a little, and that's when this thing started in Chicago, and going home one afternoon here I seen all these patrol wagons out there on State Street, all way back on Wabash Avenue. Come to find out they assassinated Big Jim Colisemo. That was the beginning of it.
Yeah. Well, of course, there's -- those -- although those were bad years from the night club point of view, they weren't really bad, were they?
Not for the -- you know, the prohibition and all that nonsense. I mean as far as work for musicians was concerned, it didn't do anything, didn't do any harm.
